function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to execute shell commands or interact with external systems (GitHub, Docker, etc.) from here, but I can walk you through exactly what you need to do on your own machine and give you ready‑to‑paste templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Open the folder in your favourite editor (VS Code, Vim, etc.) and look at:

| File | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Entry point (`main`), scripts (`start`, `dev`), dependencies |
| `src/` or `app.js` | Where the server starts, which port it listens on |
| `.env.example` | Environment variables that might be required |
| `README.md` | Any hints about deployment or runtime requirements |

> **Common findings for a typical Node.js app**  
> * `main`: `index.js` or `app.js`  
> * `scripts.start`: `"node index.js"`  
> * Listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`  

If the repo contains a `Dockerfile` already, review it and decide whether you need to modify or replace it.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Below is a minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile for a Node.js app that listens on port 3000. Adjust the `EXPOSE` line if your app uses a different port.

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
RUN npm run build || true   # Optional: if you have a build step

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=builder /app ./
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]   # Replace with your entry point if different
```

> **Why this multi‑stage build?**  
> * Keeps the final image small (only runtime deps).  
> * Allows you to run a build step if your project compiles TypeScript, bundles assets, etc.

If the repo already has a Dockerfile that looks fine, you can skip this step.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a new directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) inside the repo:

```bash
mkdir k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "128Mi"
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – Point to the image you’ll push to GitHub Container Registry or Docker Hub.  
> * `replicas:` – Scale as needed.  
> * `resources:` – Tune CPU/memory limits for your cluster.

### 2.4 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed for GHCR
      id-token: write   # Needed for OIDC auth

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache node modules
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:buildcache
        cache-to: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:buildcache,mode=max

    - name: Verify image digest
      run: echo "Image pushed with digest ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}"
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication to GHCR.  
> * Caches `node_modules` to speed up subsequent builds.  
> * Pushes the image to GHCR under the same name as the repo.  
> * Optionally caches Docker layers via GHCR (requires GHCR cache support).

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you modified an existing Dockerfile, just `git add Dockerfile` again.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run.  
> * Once it succeeds, the Docker image will be available at `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Repo cloned |
| ✅ | Dockerfile created/updated |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` added |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` added |
| ✅ | Files staged (`git add`) |
| ✅ | Commit & push (`git commit && git push`) |

---

That’s all you need to do. Once the workflow finishes, you’ll have a fully CI‑enabled Node.js repo with Docker and Kubernetes artefacts ready for deployment. Happy coding!
